source.title: The Linear Centroids Hypothesis: Features as Directions Learned by Local Experts
source.authors: Thomas Walker; Ahmed Imtiaz Humayun; Randall Balestriero; R. Baraniuk

record.tranche_reason: Compares SAE feature correspondence across DINO models using maximum cosine similarity, bearing on the stability aspect of V5 with a measure different from the original toy-model superposition setup.
record.gate_note: The study does not test sparse feature superposition under a feature-count-versus-dimension constraint, polysemanticity caused by capacity pressure, or one-dimensional superposed features. Its cross-model SAE dictionary comparison bears on V5's stability aspect; the other SAE results concern downstream accuracy and activation frequency, not whether SAE features are complete or canonical units.
record.test_reason: The study argues that SAE features built on intermediate activations are partly spurious. It shows this with DINOv2 SAE features that often fail to match DINOv3 SAE features (Fig. 4, third panel). That is a specific, if weak, argument against V5's stability and canonicity. Most other results compare the authors' centroid method with standard SAEs on downstream performance.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right but narrow. The authors conclude that centroids, not activations, should be the substrate for interpretability tools. On DINO, centroid-based SAE dictionaries generalize better, have more active features, and align across DINOv2 and DINOv3. Activation-based features they partly attribute to spurious artifacts. They also claim LCH suppresses spurious features, aids GPT2 circuit discovery, improves probe generalization in Llama-3.1-8B, and gives faithful saliency maps.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares centroid-based and intermediate-activation SAE dictionaries across DINO models; it does not reproduce the original toy-model superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: Feature correspondence differs between centroid-based and intermediate-activation dictionaries.

fits_no_version.finding: SAEs trained on centroids give higher downstream probe accuracy and more features active on test inputs than SAEs trained on activations (Fig. 4, first and second panels; Fig. 12).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE dictionaries from intermediate activations contain more rarely-firing or downstream-useless features than mapping-aware alternatives.

fits_no_version.finding: Linear probes on activations recover a color feature even when it is spurious, while centroid probes recover it only when it is task-relevant (Fig. 3, third panel).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Linear directions in activations can encode features the network does not use.

record.problems: For the V5-relevant comparison, the reported measure is maximum cosine similarity and the text gives only qualitative descriptions plus an approximate value for a large proportion of the LRH features. The comparison does not establish feature completeness or canonical status.

untested.parts: Completeness of SAE features, stability across seeds or dictionary sizes within one model, and canonicity tests such as feature splitting or meta-SAEs. Only the cross-model correspondence of cls-token SAEs was tested.
Not tested: no toy superposition setup, sparsity transition or feature geometry.
Not tested: the SAE experiments use DINO vision models, and no evidence on LLM features being distributed or SAE-recoverable is reported.
Not tested: linear directions are assumed, and multi-dimensional features are not examined.

record.verdict_notes: Preprint. The V5-relevant evidence is a single figure panel without numbers, error bars or a chance baseline. It cites Toy Models of Superposition only as the LRH reference and is not an original source. Whether DINOv2 and DINOv3 SAE decoder directions can be compared by cosine directly is not addressed, so treat r2 cautiously.

versions.untested_parts: Whether sparse features exceeding network dimensions are stored as overlapping, nearly orthogonal directions, and how sparsity affects that geometry.
Whether polysemanticity results from limited capacity and whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise without capacity pressure or are evidence of superposition.
The version concerns indirect evidence in LLMs; the SAE dictionary experiments reported here use DINO vision models.
The cross-model cosine comparison bears on feature correspondence/stability only; it does not establish that SAE features are complete or canonical units.
The study proposes linear directions as features but does not test whether features involved in superposition are one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.

rows.subject: DINOv2
rows.operation_detail: Compared each DINOv2 SAE feature's maximum cosine similarity with the full DINOv3 dictionary.
rows.measure: Maximum cosine similarity of each DINOv2 feature with features in the DINOv3 dictionary
rows.value: High cosine similarities; exact values not stated
rows.note: The authors describe centroid-based dictionaries as aligning across DINOv2 and DINOv3.
rows.check: This row measures SAEs trained on centroids, the study's own method. V5 concerns dictionary features of the model's activations, so this row is a method comparison, not evidence on V5. No numeric value is given; it is read only from a figure.

rows.subject: DINOv2
rows.operation_detail: Compared each DINOv2 SAE feature's maximum cosine similarity with the full DINOv3 dictionary.
rows.measure: Maximum cosine similarity of each DINOv2 feature with features in the DINOv3 dictionary
rows.value: A large proportion of features have cosine similarities around 0.4; the distribution is described as bimodal
rows.note: The authors state that these features do not correlate across the models; the reported around-0.4 value applies to a large proportion, not necessarily the entire dictionary.
rows.check: The value is qualitative: a bimodal distribution, with 'a large proportion' of features near 0.4 maximum cosine similarity. Some features match well, so cross-model correspondence is partial, not absent. The baseline is the centroid method, not a null or chance level. Per Appendix H, the SAEs were trained on the cls token only. It is not explained how DINOv2 and DINOv3 decoder directions are put in a common basis before computing cosine similarity. Cross-model comparison also differs from seed or size stability within one model.

relationships.condition: TopK SAEs on DINOv2 vs DINOv3 cls-token activations from the last MLP block, Imagenette
relationships.reason: The cosine-similarity distribution is bimodal, with many features near 0.4. The authors read the unmatched features as spurious, so cross-model correspondence is only partial (r2). The evidence is qualitative and the cross-model basis alignment is unclear.
relationships.display_finding: Cosine similarities between the two models' features were bimodal with many near 0.4, which the authors read as spurious features, though the evidence is qualitative and cross-model basis alignment is unclear.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Centroid-based SAE dictionaries compared across DINOv2 and DINOv3
reader_labels.reason: The authors report high cross-model feature cosine similarities, supporting correspondence in this setting (r1).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Intermediate-activation (LRH) SAE dictionaries compared across DINOv2 and DINOv3
reader_labels.reason: The authors report that the features do not correlate across models and that many similarities are around 0.4, challenging cross-model stability in this setting (r2).
